about: Bengaluru: who is doing what about heat? (/cities/bengaluru/who-is-doing-what/), November 2026. Each claim is tied to the exact words its source has to hold; stage.js stages the sources in data/inbox/2026-11-bengaluru-ecosystem/, verify-sources.yml checks them, and gate.js writes confirmed.json. Only confirmed claims reach the page and the shared records. Researched 28 November 2026 from public sources only; no organisation was contacted. Pages that could not be read during research (HeatWatch's Google Drive PDFs, the Deccan Herald and The Hindu pages, which refused automated readers, and the Karnataka Heat Action Plan 2026, whose server returned 503) are staged where a claim might still rest on them, and the gate decides. After the first check (28 November 2026): WRI India's forum thread serves only its first posts to an automated reader, so the claims from later posts are staged on each post's plain-text address; The Week returned Access Denied, so the city corporations claim rests on The Federal's report; the Karnataka Heat Action Plan 2026 (server error), C40's accelerator report (blocked) and the report PDF on Hasiru Dala's site (served an empty page) are held back.

claims.text: The Bengaluru Heat Collective was launched in Bengaluru on 15 July 2026 by 11 organisations, as a platform to advance coordinated action on rising urban heat.
rests_on: coordinated action on rising urban heat

claims.text: WRI India published its launch release on 17 July 2026, two days after the event.
The 11 founding members named at launch: ARTPARK, Bengaluru Sustainability Forum, C40 Cities, CSTEP, Hasiru Dala, HeatWatch, Jan Sahas, KHPT, NIMHANS, Socratus and WRI India.

KHPT's announcement gives fuller names for several members: C40 Cities South and West Asia, Center for Study of Science, Technology and Policy, Jan Sahas Foundation, NIMHANS, Bangalore, and Socratus Collective Wisdom Corporation; it describes KHPT as a founding partner.
rests_on: C40 Cities South and West Asia
Center for Study of Science, Technology and Policy

claims.text: KHPT posted its announcement on 17 July 2026.

For its initial phase the Collective named four priority areas: understanding heat and its spatial dimensions to inform policy and investment; enabling infrastructure interventions; strengthening relief and resilience measures for vulnerable communities; and advancing ward-level microplanning.

KHPT describes the same four areas as mapping heat risk across the city, building cooling infrastructure such as shade, shelters and hydration points, strengthening health monitoring and protections for outdoor and informal workers, and developing ward level microplans.

A WRI India partner update after the launch reports that the members agreed a Charter document for the group to function as a collective body, and that a Strategy Note on heat resilience in Bengaluru was developed as a living document. Neither document was found published.
A later partner update reports that the Collective convened in August 2026 to begin developing a theory of change and a strategic workplan.
The launch notice described a panel on lived experiences of heat and a charter signing at Science Gallery Bengaluru.
At the launch, an ASHA worker, a domestic worker, a construction worker and a waste picker spoke about heat in their work.
Officials of Bengaluru North City Corporation, Bengaluru South City Corporation and NIUA's Climate Centre for Cities spoke at the launch.

On 14 July 2026 the city observatory recorded 33.6°C, which WRI India, citing the India Meteorological Department, describes as Bengaluru's highest July temperature on record, above 33.3°C set in 1914 and 1926.

At the launch, the Commissioner of Bengaluru North City Corporation referred to ₹5 crore allocated for heat resilience by an NIUA pilot, under the Building Heat Resilient Cities Programme of AMRUT 2.0. The figure is attributed to that statement; no sanction order was found.
Of that ₹5 crore, ₹1 crore was described as dedicated to protecting vulnerable populations, such as safety gear for outdoor informal workers. It is part of the ₹5 crore, not an addition to it.
NIUA's Climate Centre for Cities said the heat resilience proposal was submitted by Bengaluru North City Corporation.
rests_on: submitted by Bengaluru North City Corporation

claims.text: The Commissioner described roof coating demonstrations on North City Corporation buildings as planned. No completed installation was found reported.
An independent report of the launch says the ₹1 crore would go to safety gear and neck fans for outdoor informal workers, and mentions albedo coating demonstrations.

Bengaluru South City Corporation (BSCC) announced ₹2 crore allocated for phased implementation of the Begur Ward Climate Action Plan, covering heat proofing of buildings, blue-green schools and groundwater recharge, and its Chief Engineer called it not a final budget but a starting point. Not all of it is heat-specific.

WRI India's partner update says the Begur plan's enabling work was steered by WRI India with working group members Jan Sahas, WellLabs, Hasiru Dala, Socratus, CSTEP and Sensing Local, and that BSCC introduced it at the Collective's launch.

WRI India's partner update of 27 June 2026 reports that four of the five municipal corporations allocated about ₹52 crore in total directly towards climate action in their 2026-27 budgets. This is climate spending in general, not heat spending.

WRI India reports a pipeline of 302 projects (182 for the South and 120 for the North City Corporation), co-developed with more than ten organisations for the 2026-27 Climate Action Plan and formally submitted to the corporations.

Ward-level climate action plans are led by the Bengaluru Climate Action Cell under the Greater Bengaluru Authority, with five pilot wards, one per zone: Shantinagar, Jakkur, Begur, Vijinapura and Nalwadi Krishnaraja Wadiyar. Public consultations were held in all five.
Heat is not one of the plans' seven sectors; local heat maps were among the data gathered, and residents mapped cool spaces in Jakkur.

Mongabay India reported in March 2026 that the older administrative body had allocated ₹28 crore for climate action and that the new zone-wise budgets were yet to be released; Citizen Matters described the same ₹28 crore as earmarked in the 2025-26 budget for proposed ward-level plans.

Citizen Matters lists a seven-organisation working group: WRI India, Socratus Foundation, Jansahas, WellLabs, Sensing Local, CSTEP and Hasiru Dala, and reports plans for ten wards across five city corporations, starting with Shantinagar.
Mongabay India describes WELL Labs as a technical partner for the city climate plan and CSTEP as anchoring the energy sector for the ward plans.

ARTPARK, a not-for-profit company at IISc, describes sub-district heat-risk predictions up to seven days ahead, built with the Government of Karnataka (KSNDMC, KSDMA and the Department of Health). The page gives no public access link, users or accuracy figures.

claims.where: Tool: BHRIGU National Heat Insights Explorer
claims.text: CSTEP's BHRIGU project describes an open-access National Heat Insights Explorer for multi-hazard risk visualisation, and phased work in six representative urbanscapes, as outcomes envisioned. The page names neither the six places nor a live address.
CSTEP is conducting an organisational mapping exercise of actors engaged in building heat resilience in India; this profile used it as a discovery source and checked each entry separately.

CSTEP is developing an Ecosystem-based Adaptation Feasibility Tool (DEFT) for Bengaluru, extending to Bangalore Urban District, supported by IUCN under the Global EbA Fund; intended outputs include hyper-local flood and heatwave risk mapping and a blue-green infrastructure map. The page also reports a household survey across Bangalore. No live tool address is given.
CSTEP held a stakeholder engagement workshop for DEFT using Hebbal as a case study.

HeatWatch has an interactive dashboard combining temperature data with factory-level insights from India's textile and garment sector, mapping brand supply chains. A Bengaluru deployment was not found: its garment fieldwork named elsewhere is outside Bengaluru.

claims.where: Tool: Heat Safety Charter for apartment workers
claims.text: The Bangalore Apartment Federation and HeatWatch Foundation developed a Heat Safety Charter for Apartment Workers, with support from the Bangalore Sustainability Forum, setting out heat safety measures apartment communities can adopt, in English, Kannada and Hindi. No adoption figures were found.

claims.where: Tool: Heat Safety Charter for apartment workers
claims.text: The charter's measures can also support security guards, housekeeping staff, gardeners, delivery workers and drivers at apartment complexes.

A survey of 154 waste workers in Bengaluru (98 women and 56 men) by HeatWatch and Hasiru Dala found only 39.6% had access to clean drinking water and 13% to clean washrooms; free-roaming waste pickers lost an average of ₹504 a week, about 14% of income, and reported ₹1,196 a month in medical costs for heat-related illness.
Over 60% of respondents belonged to Scheduled Castes, and over 92% said heat makes their tasks harder and slower.

HeatWatch and volunteers audited parks closed between 11 AM and 4 PM and, in April 2026, asked for park hours of 5 AM to 10 PM and for parks to be treated as cooling and resting spaces. No decision was found reported.
HeatWatch has begun engaging with domestic workers in Bengaluru with the Domestic Workers Union, as an ongoing area of work.

A domestic-worker heat stress project by HeatWatch Foundation with St John's Medical College Hospital, listed among Bengaluru Sustainability Forum's supported projects, started in September 2025, with participatory research, workshops and a playbook for other cities among its planned outputs.
Bengaluru Sustainability Forum describes itself as an inter-institutional initiative; its Small Grants Programme, started in 2018, has funded over 40 projects.

With a Global Resilience Partnership award, Socratus co-designed focus group discussions with Bengaluru Sustainability Forum under its Climate Charche initiative, with domestic, gig and migrant workers, pourakarmikas and ASHA workers; water was the central theme and heat a secondary one.

The Migrants Resilience Collaborative, initiated by Jan Sahas, ran three cooling centres in Bengaluru in 2026, at a construction site in Whitefield, in Greater Bengaluru Authority facilities in Vidyaranyapura and above an Anganwadi in Allalasandra, open from 10 April to the first week of July, with drinking water, ORS, coolers, cots and first aid.
Staff at the Vidyaranyapura centre told the reporter it helped more than 10 workers apply for construction welfare cards and around 60 to register for Ayushman and e-Shram benefits.

Writing for the India Climate Collaborative, the Migrants Resilience Collaborative reports a study of over 2,300 migrant households in which 89% named heat as the main stressor, and says cooling access was first piloted in Bengaluru.

In April 2026, Hasiru Dala, C40 Cities and Sensing Local gave cooling kits to 202 workers, including 46 ASHAs, 116 pourakarmikas, 18 dry waste collection centre workers and 20 traffic police, mostly in the North City Corporation. Each kit cost about ₹2,160; an impact report was being prepared.

The project team proposed activating 63 Indira canteens across all five city corporations as public cooling centres during heat alerts; scale-up was to use funds under the national heat resilience programme of MoHUA and NIUA. Both are proposals.

C40 Cities sought technical assistance, with proposals due on 19 October 2025, to develop two High Impact Actions with detailed project reports for urban heat in identified wards of Bengaluru, working with the Greater Bengaluru Authority over about five months from November 2025.
Bengaluru is listed among the signatory cities of C40's Cool Cities Accelerator.
The Greater Bengaluru Authority's five city corporations, Bengaluru Central, North, South, East and West, came into being in September 2025.
The Karnataka Heat Action Plan 2026 includes the Greater Bengaluru area.
The report is also published on Hasiru Dala's own site.

Shantinagar's ward plan, in Bengaluru Central City Corporation, was completed and submitted to the GBA Climate Action Cell and the corporation by the seven-member working group, with WRI India anchoring the drafting. The Climate Action Cell has a ward plan webpage.
Citizen Matters reported the ₹28 crore climate earmark in the BBMP's budget for 2025-26, before the change to the Greater Bengaluru Authority.
